title.en: Fedelm the Prophetess Sees the Host Red
title.zh: 菲德爾姆預言「我見赤色」

region.en: Road to Cualnge, Co. Louth, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡通往庫爾涅之路（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (Book of the Dun Cow recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: Medb asks Fedelm, prophetess of Connaught, fresh from Scotland, to read her hosting with the imbas forosnai. Three times the maiden answers, 'I see very red, I see red,' and against Medb's objections reads the boy she sees: a fair man with a hero's flame over his head, carrying two Gae-bolga in each hand, the Riastartha the distorted one — Cuchulainn Mac Sualtaim, who will make dense slaughters of the host and leave it many thousands of heads.
summary.zh: 梅芙請剛從蘇格蘭學成歸來的康諾特女先知菲德爾姆，以「智慧之視」占看大軍。少女三次答曰：「我見赤色，我見赤色。」無視梅芙的反駁，她讀出所見少年：頭頂英雄之火的俊美者，雙手各持雙重蛙矛——「扭曲者」里亞斯塔爾塔——庫丘林。他將使大軍血染成赤，留下千萬首級。

sensitivity.note: The imbas forosnai divination is an attested Irish legal-poetic practice; the frame (prophetess who sees only blood) is the epic's doom-device. Pin symbolic at the marching route.

passages.text: 'Fedelm, the prophetess of Connaught, is my name,' said the maiden. 'Whence do you come?' 'From Scotland, after learning the art of prophecy.' 'Have you the inspiration which illumines?' 'Yes, indeed.' 'Look for me how it will be with my hosting.' Then the maiden looked for it; and Medb said: 'O Fedelm the prophetess, how seest thou the host?' Fedelm answered and said: 'I see very red, I see red.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'That is not true,' said Medb; 'for Conchobar is in his sickness at Emain and the Ulstermen with him.' 'Fedelm the prophetess, how seest thou our host?' 'I see red.' 'That matters not; for there are mutual angers and quarrels in every host. Look again for us then, and tell us the truth.' 'I see very red, I see red... I see a fair man who will make play with a number of wounds on his girdle; a hero's flame over his head, his forehead a meeting-place of victory... Like is the nature of his valour to Cuchulainn of Murthemne. I do not know whose is the Hound of Culann, whose fame is the fairest. But I know that it is thus that the host is very red from him... He will strike on whole hosts, he will make dense slaughters of you, ye will leave with him many thousands of heads.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

title.en: The Ogam Withe on the Pillar

region.en: Iraird Cuillend, Co. Meath, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭米斯郡伊拉爾德·庫倫（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (LU recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: Going to a tryst, Cuchulainn twists a spancel-withe of a single twig, writes an ogam on it, and throws it on a pillar-stone: let no one pass till a man throws a like withe with one hand, Fergus excepted. The four sons of the vanguard find it, Fergus reads the ogam, and warns: outrage this withe, and the hand of him who wrote will slay a goodly slaughter of you before morning. Ailill's host turns aside by the neck of the great wood rather than meet the geis.
summary.zh: 赴約之前，庫丘林以單枝柳條扭成繫獸環，刻歐甘文於其上，擲於石柱之頂：除非有人單手擲出同樣的環，無人可過——費爾古斯除外。前鋒四人發現此環，費爾古斯誦出歐甘之義並警告：若辱此環，刻文者的手將在黎明前屠戮你們。大軍遂繞大林而行，不敢觸犯此誓。

sensitivity.note: The withe-and-ogam geis is the Tain's master-token of single combat (compare the withe of the sons of Nechta Scene, whose removal is called a breach of geis in the Leinster gloss); ogam-writing on withe and oak recurs as Cuchulainn's road-magic. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: He made a spancel-withe then before he went — a twig twisted in the form of two rings, joined by one straight piece, as used for hobbling horses and cattle — and wrote an ogam on it, and threw it on the top of the pillar. The leadership of the way before the army was given to Fergus. Then Fergus went far astray to the south, till Ulster should have completed the collection of an army; he did this for friendship. 'O Fergus, this is strange, what kind of way do we go?... It is to avoid the great man who protects Mag Murthemne... But if perchance I may avoid even afterwards Cuchulainn Mac Sualtaim.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

passages.text: They found the withe that Cuchulainn threw, and perceived the grazing that the horses had grazed, and gave the withe into the hands of Fergus Mac Roich; he read the ogam that was on it. 'We wait because of the withe yonder. There is an ogam on it, and this is what is in it: Let no one go past till a man is found to throw a like withe with his one hand, and let it be one twig of which it is made; and I except my friend Fergus.' Then Fergus said to them: 'If you outrage this withe, or if you go past it, though he be in the custody of a man, or in a house under a lock, the hand of the man who wrote the ogam on it will reach him, and will slay a goodly slaughter of you before morning, unless one of you throw a like withe.' 'It does not please us, indeed, that one of us should be slain at once,' said Ailill. 'We will go by the neck of the great wood yonder, south of us, and we will not go over it at all.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

region.en: Fort of the sons of Nechta Scene, Co. Louth, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡涅克塔之子堡壘（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (LU recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: Cuchulainn reaches the fort of Foill, Fandall and Tuachell, who say there are not more of the Ulstermen alive than they have slain, and breaks their withe into the stream — a breach of their geis. Sleeping by the pillar he bids the charioteer wake him not for few but for many; Foill's back is broken by the first spear, Fandall the Swallow is taken in the ford, and the javelin makes a red-sieve of Tuachell the Cunning. With three heads and a live deer and a flock of swans in the chariot he rides for Emain, where the naked women of the court must meet him before the heroes can seize him.
summary.zh: 庫丘林抵達福伊爾、凡達爾、圖阿凱爾三兄弟之堡——他們自誇所殺的阿爾斯特人不比餘下的少。他擲其柳環入溪流，破了兄弟們的誓約。倚柱而眠前囑咐車伕：「非多人勿醒我。」福伊爾首矛即斃；「燕」凡達爾殞於淺灘；一矛使「狡者」圖阿凱爾化為紅篩。攜三首級、活鹿與天鵝群馳向埃馬因——唯有裸身的宮中女子現身，英雄們方能將他制服。

sensitivity.note: The withe removed is explicitly a breach of geis in the Leinster gloss; the naked-women cooling is the standard riastrad (warp-spasm) control device — the boy-hero's heat quenched in vessels of water. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: They reached the fort of the three sons of Nechta Scene; Foill, Fandall, and Tuachell were their names. 'Is it they who say that there are not more of the Ulstermen alive than they have slain of them?' 'It is they indeed.' 'Let us go till we reach them.' 'Truly it is not to avoid it that we go.' Then they go forth, and he threw the withe that was on the pillar as far as he could throw into the river, for this was a breach of geis to the sons of Nechta Scene. They perceive it then, and come to them. Cuchulainn goes to sleep by the pillar after throwing the withe at the stream; and he said to the charioteer: 'Do not waken me for few; but waken me for many.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'Take heed of the man who comes against you. Foill is his name, for unless you reach him in the first thrust, you will not reach him till evening.' Then he cast the spear at him, so that his back broke. 'Take heed of another man, Fandall is his name. Not more heavily does he traverse the water than swan or swallow.' They meet then in the ford; Cuchulainn kills that man, and took his head and his arms. 'Take heed of another man who comes towards you. Tuachell is his name. It is no misname for him, for he does not fall by arms at all.' 'Here is the javelin for him to confuse him, so that it may make a red-sieve of him.' He cast the spear at him, and cut off his head. He heard then the cry of their mother, Nechta Scene, behind them, and put their spoils and the three heads in his chariot.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

passages.text: They go on to Sliab Fuait, and Cuchulainn seized the deer that was nearest and finest of the herd and bound it between the two poles of the chariot, and struck eight swans with a small stone and twelve with a large, all by his return stroke, and bound the birds from the strings and thongs of the chariot; so that it was thus he went to Emain Macha: the wild deer behind his chariot, and the flock of swans flying over it, and the three heads in his chariot. 'A man in a chariot is coming to you; he will shed the blood of every man who is in the court, unless naked women go to him.' Then the women of Emain go to meet him with Mugain, the wife of Conchobar Mac Nessa, and bare their breasts before him: 'These are the warriors who will meet you to-day.' He covers his face; then the heroes of Emain seize him and throw him into a vessel of cold water. That vessel bursts round him. The second vessel boiled with bubbles as big as the fist therefrom. The third vessel into which he went he warmed so that its heat and its cold were rightly tempered; and he sits at Conchobar's knee, and that was his couch always after that. 'The man who did this in his seventh year, it were not wonderful though he should rout an overwhelming force when his seventeen years are complete to-day.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

title.en: The Drowning of Fraech at the Ford

region.en: Ath Fraich (Fraech's Ford), Co. Louth, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡弗蕾赫渡口（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (LU recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: Medb begs Fraech to remove the strait from the host, and he goes to Ath Fuait with nine men and finds Cuchulainn bathing. 'Do not come to me; you will die from it, and I should be sorry to kill you.' 'I shall come indeed, that we may meet in the water; and let your play with me be fair.' They wrestle long on the water; twice Cuchulainn lifts him up and twice Fraech refuses to yield, and the third time he is held under until he is killed. A troop of women in green tunics — his kin of the Sid, Bebind's sister being Boinn herself — draw his body away into a mound called after him, Sid Fraich.
summary.zh: 梅芙懇求弗蕾赫為大軍解圍；他攜九人至阿特·福伊特，見庫丘林正在河中沐浴。「別過來——你會送命，殺你我也痛心。」「我偏要來，讓我們在水中相會；且望你對我手下留情。」二人在水中長久角力；庫丘林兩度將他托起，弗蕾赫兩度拒絕認輸，第三次被按入水中至死。一隊綠衣女子——其仙族血親（貝賓德之妹即博因河本身）——將他的屍身引入以他命名的仙丘。

sensitivity.note: Fraech (Fráech mac Idaid) is the demi-divine Fenian-linked hero of the Ulster cycle (his raiment of Alban treasure, Findabair episode); the water-wrestling death with yield-refusal is the fixed ford-combat pattern that Fer Diad's episode repeats at scale. The fairy women bearing the body to a sid is the mortality-undoing motif. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: They are there till next morning; then Fraech is summoned to them. 'Help us, O Fraech,' said Medb. 'Remove from us the strait that is on us. Go before Cuchulainn for us, if perchance you shall fight with him.' He set out early in the morning with nine men, till he reached Ath Fuait. He saw the warrior bathing in the river. 'Wait here, till I come to the man yonder; not good is the water,' said he. He took off his clothes, and goes into the water to him. 'Do not come to me,' said Cuchulainn. 'You will die from it, and I should be sorry to kill you.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I shall come indeed, that we may meet in the water; and let your play with me be fair.' 'Settle it as you like.' 'The hand of each of us round the other,' said Fraech. They set to wrestling for a long time on the water, and Fraech was submerged. Cuchulainn lifted him up again. 'This time, will you yield and accept your life?' 'I will not suffer it,' said Fraech. Cuchulainn put him under it again, until Fraech was killed. He comes to land; his retinue carry his body to the camp. Ath Fraich, that was the name of that ford for ever. All the host lamented Fraech. They saw a troop of women in green tunics on the body of Fraech Mac Idaid — for Fraech was descended from the people of the Sid, his mother Bebind being a fairy woman, and her sister was Boinn, the river Boyne — they drew him from them into the mound; Sid Fraich was the name of that mound afterwards.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

title.en: The Morrigan Offers Love and Threatens Shapes
title.zh: 摩里岡示愛與化身威脅

region.en: Ath Grencha (Ath Darteisc), Co. Louth, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡格倫哈渡口（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (LU recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: A young woman in a dress of every colour comes to Cuchulainn — daughter of Buan the king, she says — with her treasures and her cattle: 'I have loved you for your reputation.' 'The time at which you have come to us is not good; our condition is evil through hunger.' Then she names her threats: an eel about his feet in the ford; a grey she-wolf driving the cattle on him; a hornless red heifer rushing on him at the pools. He answers each: broken ribs between his toes, an eye broken with a sling-stone, a leg broken — till a doom of blessing comes on her.
summary.zh: 一位身披百色衣裙的少女向庫丘林走來——自稱王者布安之女，攜財富牛群：「我因你的名聲而愛你。」「此時非相見之時；我軍困於飢餓。」她一一陳其威脅：化作鰻魚纏足使其跌倒；化為灰母狼驅牛群衝撞；化為無角赤牝犢於水潭前突襲。他一一作答：趾間斷其肋骨、彈石碎其一目、斷其一腿——直到「吉運之命降於她」。

sensitivity.note: The Morrigan's courtship-refusal is the Tain's great theomachy hinge (she then fights him as a bird at the ford and is wounded); her eel-wolf-heifer shape-threats are a fixed triple-transformation set-piece. The 'doom of blessing' clause licenses her later healing. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: Cuchulainn saw a young woman coming towards him, with a dress of every colour on, and her form very excellent. 'Who are you?' 'Daughter of Buan the king. I have come to you; I have loved you for your reputation, and I have brought my treasures and my cattle with me.' 'The time at which you have come to us is not good. For our condition is evil, through hunger. It is not easy to me to meet a woman, while I am in this strife.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'I will be a help to you... I shall be more troublesome to you when I come against you when you are in combat against the men. I will come in the form of an eel about your feet in the ford, so that you shall fall.' 'I will take you between my toes, till your ribs are broken, and you will be in this condition till a doom of blessing comes on you.' 'I will drive the cattle on the ford to you, in the form of a grey she-wolf.' 'I will throw a stone at you from my sling, so that it shall break your eye in your head.' 'I will come to you in the form of a hornless red heifer before the cattle. They will rush on you on the plains and on the fords, and you will not see me before you.' 'I will throw a stone at you, so that your leg shall break under you, and you will be in this state till a doom of blessing comes on you.' Therewith she goes from him.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

title.en: The Healing of the Morrigan from the Three-Teat Cow
title.zh: 以三乳牛之奶醫治摩里岡

region.en: Tarthesc, Mag Murthemne, Co. Louth, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡穆瑟姆尼平原（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (LU recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: Worn out with battle, Cuchulainn meets an old hag, blind and lame, milking a cow with three teats, and asks a drink. 'He will be whole who has brought it; the blessings of gods and non-gods on you' — the gods with them the Mighty Folk of the Sid, the non-gods the people of husbandry. Milk of the first teat heals her head, of the second her eye, of the third her leg: 'You told me I should not have healing from you for ever.' 'If I had known it was you, I would not have healed you ever.'
summary.zh: 戰疲力竭之際，庫丘林遇見一位盲且跛的老嫗，正擠一頭有三乳的牛，他索水解渴。「帶來者必得痊愈；願神與非神賜福於你。」——彼所謂神即仙丘的「偉大之民」，非神即務農之民。第一乳之奶愈其頭，第二乳愈其目，第三乳愈其腿。「你曾說我永不得你的醫治。」「早知是你，我永遠不會治你。」

sensitivity.note: The milk-healing that undoes the healing-words is the inverse of the usual blessing-cure — the drinker's 'whole' pronouncement becomes the goddess's cure; gods and non-gods is the redactor's gloss on pre-Christian cult vocabulary. Tagged 'resurrection' for the wound-to-whole function as elsewhere in the corpus.

passages.text: When Cuchulainn was in this great weariness, the Morrigan met him in the form of an old hag, and she blind and lame, milking a cow with three teats, and he asked her for a drink. She gave him milk from a teat. 'He will be whole who has brought it,' said Cuchulainn; 'the blessings of gods and non-gods on you.' The gods with them were the Mighty Folk, the dwellers in the Sid; non-gods the people of husbandry. Then her head was healed so that it was whole.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

passages.text: She gave the milk of the second teat, and her eye was whole; and gave the milk of the third teat, and her leg was whole; and this was what he said about each thing of them, 'A doom of blessing on you.' 'You told me,' said the Morrigan, 'I should not have healing from you for ever.' 'If I had known it was you,' said Cuchulainn, 'I would not have healed you ever.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

title.en: Lug of the Sid Heals His Son in Sleep
title.zh: 仙丘的魯格為其子催眠療傷

region.en: Mound in Lerga, Mag Murthemne, Co. Louth, Ireland (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 愛爾蘭勞斯郡勒爾加丘（象徵定位）

texts.period: Tain Bo Cuailnge (LU recension), trans. L. Winifred Faraday (1904)

source.work: L. Winifred Faraday, The Cattle-Raid of Cualnge (1904), eBook #21557

summary.en: Alone against the four provinces of Ireland, Cuchulainn sees a fair tall warrior crossing the hostile camp unattacked and attacking no one: 'Which of my friends from the Sid is that who comes to have pity on me?' 'It is I, your father from the Sid, Lug Mac Ethlend. Sleep a little, O Cuchulainn, till the end of three days and three nights, and I will fight against the hosts for that space.' He sings the ferdord and casts herbs of curing into the wounds; and in those three days the boys of Emain give three battles and fall but Folloman Mac Conchobair, who dies boasting he would take Ailill's crowned head.
summary.zh: 獨對愛爾蘭四省大軍的庫丘林，見一名俊美高挑的戰士穿行敵營而無人察覺：「是仙丘中哪位故友前來憐憫我？」「我是你仙丘的父親，埃斯倫之子魯格。睡吧，三日三夜，我代你迎戰大軍。」他以費爾多德咒文催眠，將療傷草藥投入傷口；三日間，埃馬因的少年軍三戰三敗，唯福洛曼戰亡——他至死誇言要取埃利爾的金冠首級。

sensitivity.note: Lug Mac Ethlend's paternity of Cuchulainn (the god as absent father from the Sid) is the mythic core of the Ulster hero; the three-day sleep with god-guarded healing is the cycle's great restorative hinge — the Sleeping Beauty shape in heroic form. The boys' battle is the pathos-counterpoint. Pin symbolic.

passages.text: Then the four provinces of Ireland took camp in the Breslech Mor in Mag Murthemne, and Cuchulainn took his post at the mound in Lerga near them, and his charioteer Loeg Mac Riangabra kindled a fire for him. He saw the fiery sheen of the bright golden arms over the heads of the four provinces of Ireland at the setting of the clouds of evening, and fury and great rage came over him; he uttered his hero's shout from his throat, so that goblins and sprites and spectres of the glen and demons of the air answered, and the Nemain produced confusion on the host, so that a hundred warriors of them died of terror and of heart-burst in the middle of the camp. When Loeg was there, he saw something: a single man who came straight across the camp of the men of Ireland from the north-east, a man fair and tall, with waving yellow hair, a green mantle folded round him, and a five-pointed spear in his hand. 'Which of my friends from the Sid is that who comes to have pity on me, because they know the sore distress in which I am, alone against the four great provinces of Ireland?'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'It is I, your father from the Sid, Lug Mac Ethlend.' 'My wounds are heavy, it were high time that I should be healed.' 'Sleep a little, O Cuchulainn, your heavy swoon of sleep at the mound of Lerga till the end of three days and three nights, and I will fight against the hosts for that space.' Then he sings the ferdord to him, and he sleeps from it; and for three days and three nights Cuchulainn was asleep — for from the Monday after the end of summer to the Wednesday after Candlemas, for that space he had not slept, except a little while against his spear after midday, with his head on his clenched fist, and his clenched fist on his spear, and his spear on his knee; but he was striking and cutting and attacking and slaying the four great provinces of Ireland for that space. It is then that the warrior of the Sid cast herbs and grasses of curing and charms of healing into the hurts and wounds and injuries of Cuchulainn, so that Cuchulainn recovered in his sleep without his perceiving it at all.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.

passages.text: Now it was at this time that the boys came south from Emain Macha: Folloman Mac Conchobair with three fifties of kings' sons of Ulster, and they gave battle thrice to the hosts, so that three times their own number fell, and all the boys fell except Folloman Mac Conchobair. Folloman boasted that he would not go back to Emain for ever and ever until he should take the head of Ailill with him, with the golden crown that was above it; but the two sons of Bethe Mac Bain came on him and wounded him so that he fell by them. So that that is the death of the boys of Ulster and of Folloman Mac Conchobair. Cuchulainn arose then from his sleep, and put his hand over his face, and made a purple wheelbeam from head to foot: 'Pity for that, that I was not in my strength! For if I had been in my strength, the boys would not have fallen as they have fallen.' 'Strive further, O Little Hound, it is no reproach to thy honour and no disgrace to thy valour.'
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Faraday 1904, LU recension; not verbatim.
